headings.title: Introduction to the Living Will Movement
headings.content: The living will movement represents a profound shift in healthcare, moving away from strict medical paternalism toward honoring personal choices at the end of life. At its core, the movement asserts that individuals possess the fundamental right to direct their own medical treatment, particularly when they become incapacitated. This social and legal advocacy framework emerged to prevent unwanted, invasive, and prolonged technological interventions when recovery is no longer possible. For nurses practicing in Nigeria and globally, understanding this movement is vital because it bridges the gap between clinical capability and human dignity.

headings.title: Historical Evolution and Milestones
headings.content: The living will concept did not appear overnight; it evolved through landmark legal cases and societal activism. In 1967, an attorney named Luis Kutner first proposed the concept of a living will as a legal instrument. Decades later, high-profile court cases, such as the legal battles surrounding Karen Ann Quinlan and Nancy Cruzan in the United States, brought public attention to the tragedy of being kept alive on machines with no hope of recovery. These legal milestones forced legislatures to create formal frameworks that recognized advance directives, slowly transforming a moral ideal into recognized legal protection.

headings.title: Living Wills versus Durable Power of Attorney
headings.content:
Advance directives generally comprise two distinct legal instruments that serve complementary functions:

- **Living Will**: A written document specifying exact treatments a person wants or refuses, such as mechanical ventilation, tube feeding, or cardiopulmonary resuscitation, specifically applicable in terminal illness or persistent vegetative states.
- **Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare**: A legal designation naming a proxy or surrogate decision-maker to speak on the patient's behalf if they become incapacitated and face choices not explicitly covered in the living will.

headings.title: Patient Autonomy and Informed Consent
headings.content: Informed consent forms the bedrock of ethical nursing practice, granting competent adults the absolute right to accept or refuse medical therapies. This autonomy does not vanish simply because a patient loses consciousness or cognitive capacity. Advance directives serve as an extension of informed consent into the future. By documenting preferences ahead of time, patients exercise prospective autonomy, ensuring that their personal values continue to govern their care even when they can no longer voice a decision.

headings.title: Challenges and Barriers to Implementation
headings.content: Despite broad ethical agreement on patient autonomy, putting advance directives into practice faces significant hurdles. Cultural and religious beliefs heavily influence how families view death and dying, often conflicting with individualistic legal frameworks. Many patients find it emotionally difficult to discuss mortality, leading to a lack of documentation. Furthermore, vagueness in living wills—such as requesting 'no heroic measures' without defining what those measures are—leaves clinicians guessing during critical moments. Institutional inertia and lack of staff training further complicate enforcement.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Advocating for Advance Directives
headings.content: Nurses occupy a unique position at the bedside, acting as the primary bridge between patients, families, and the medical team. Because nurses spend the most time with patients, they often initiate sensitive conversations about end-of-life goals before a crisis occurs. Advocating for advance directives means ensuring that patient preferences are documented in the medical record, communicated during shift handovers, and respected by incoming physicians. When family members panic during a downturn, the nurse provides reassurance by grounding care plans in the documented wishes of the patient.
